methodological_questions: how to measure shot mix (play type classification reliability)
how to isolate personnel effects from confounding (talent, opponent, game state)
natural experiment design for lineup changes (substitution windows, staggered rotations)
statistical power for detecting small shifts in play type proportions
how to handle multiple play types and multiplicity

historical_evidence.finding: Opponent lineup adaptation: shot mix when opposing rim big is off floor. DRIVE +0.82pp, POST_UP +0.43pp, 3PA -1.79pp, but rim <=4ft only +0.12pp (t=0.4), PPP +0.008 (t=1.1). Verdict WEAK/SMALL, will not carry a paper. N=1.07M possessions.

PULL_UP exposure-effect diagnostics. With lineup FE slope -0.0255 (SE 0.0061); without lineup FE -0.0063 (0.0036); placebo other play types -0.0075 (0.0017). Effect shrinks without lineup FE and same-shooter placebo consistent with shooter-level confound.

Within-game tactical adaptation (halftime, crunch, post-run). OTHER +2.26 to +2.48pp in H2 every bucket; crunch OTHER +6.08pp, PULL_UP +1.20pp at -0.045 PPP; post-run DRIVE +3.75pp, OTHER -6.72pp. No inferential tests; OTHER label known to be noisy (PT audit).
Team-season defensive H2-adjustment reliability. H2-change trait r=-0.001 (p<.05 needs ~0.18). H1 defensive level r=+0.356 (test works). Split-half r=-0.001.
Final checks: Design 5 placebo, defensive H2-adjustment trait reliability, start-of-half dip. Split-half (odd/even game) reliability of team-season H2-H1 change; no log saved.

Defensive reorganizer 28-cell signature. Gate/test3: mean DA_def 0.0712 vs null 0.0874 (paired t=-11.20); size-adjusted split-half rho=-0.083 (p=0.00729); trade portability n=175 cosine +0.2401. Artifact found.
After-timeout tactical play-type shift. POST_UP +2.406 (t=+18.7), SPOT_UP +2.333 (t=+12.9); half-court PPP -0.0105 (SE 0.0056, t=-1.89). 56,423 ATO possessions.

Connector tangible impact. Star dTS +0.05 pp p=0.937; dTO +0.74 pp p=0.00364 (wrong sign). HasConn on-off PPP BOTH_NULL (mean -0.041 p=0.939, median +0.528 p=0.731, n=73). Lineup ORtg lift is talent confound (p=0.51 after TALENT; swap p=0.565).

TOV_FORCE matchup decomposition on four playoff games. Team-PT lifts small; player-channel lifts large on small n (Banchero on Huerter SPOT_UP +8.4pp, n_def=17 / n_off=54). Cell n often 15-54 defensive possessions.

Defensive in-game adaptation to repeated play type. League-wide within-game -0.0019 PPP/exposure (SE 0.0019); only PULL_UP within-game -0.030 SE [cut]. Team trait split-half r +0.008, season-to-season +0.037.

failed_approaches.what_failed: using lineup fixed effects to isolate defensive adaptation from shooter selection
failed_approaches.why: lineup FE introduced confound; without FE effect disappeared and same-shooter placebo gave similar effect, indicating shooter-level confound (C_artifact)

failed_approaches.what_failed: trying to measure team-level defensive in-game adjustment as a reliable trait
failed_approaches.why: split-half reliability r=-0.001, making it untestable; low measurement reliability and mechanical floor

failed_approaches.what_failed: attempting to detect a defensive reorganizer signature on opponent offense
failed_approaches.why: the apparent effect was below null and split-half reliability was negative, indicating an artifact of selection/construction

failed_approaches.what_failed: measuring lineup-level connector effect on offensive efficiency
failed_approaches.why: found null after controlling for talent; apparent lineup lift was a talent confound

failed_approaches.what_failed: decomposing TOV_FORCE into individual matchups with four games of data
failed_approaches.why: exposure sparsity (cell n often 15-54) made primary defender attribution unreliable

evidence_establishes: shot mix shifts due to a single player change (opponent big off) are small (ppp ~0.008, rim share +0.12pp with SE 0.295) despite large sample
effects on specific play types (PULL_UP) can be confounded by shooter identity and disappear when controlling for shooter or when looking at placebo play types
play-type classification noise (particularly OTHER) reduces reliability and can inflate apparent shifts
in-game tactical events (timeouts) produce measurable play-type mix changes (POST_UP +2.4pp, SPOT_UP +2.3pp), showing the data can detect some shifts
lineup-level effects on offensive performance often look like talent confounds when not properly isolated
evidence_does_not_establish: whether a full offensive line change (all five players) causally changes shot mix beyond talent composition
the magnitude or sign of any such effect for the modern NBA 2022-25 seasons
that a design controlling for talent and using a natural experiment with full substitutions can achieve adequate power
that play-type shares can be reliably measured for all types without the OTHER noise problem
own_inferences: A full five-player substitution is a much stronger shock than a single-player opponent change, so effect sizes could be larger, but confounding by talent is severe because the new five usually differs in average skill

A difference-in-differences design comparing post-substitution possessions to pre-substitution possessions matched on opponent and game state can reduce some confounds but may still be biased by the reasons for the substitution (fatigue, foul trouble, blowout)

The timeout event (which shifts shot mix) can serve as a placebo or benchmark: if a full offensive change produces a shot mix shift no larger than a timeout, it will be hard to attribute to personnel synergy
Power is likely adequate only for large effects (2+ percentage point shifts in major play types), which may be unrealistic given prior small estimates
uncertainties: the number of usable full offensive five changes in three seasons and whether they occur in competitive non-garbage-time situations
the appropriate definition of shot mix (which play type taxonomy, whether to exclude OTHER or pool rare types)
the stability of play type labels across tracking systems and seasons
the optimal window length (number of possessions post-substitution) to measure the sustained effect

historical_effect.explanation: Prior work found that lineup-related shot mix effects (opponent big off) are tiny, talent confounds explain apparent effects (pull-up adaptation, connector impact), play-type measurement contains noise (OTHER), and in-game shift reliability is near zero. This shifts the decision from a straightforward test to a high-risk study requiring careful design and cautious interpretation.

blocking_constraints.text: The new offensive five differs in average talent and individual play-type preferences; without a control for talent, any observed shift is likely a selection effect rather than a synergy effect.
Some play types (especially OTHER) have high classification noise, which could mask or inflate shifts.
Full five changes may be rare in tight games; even with 1M+ possessions, the number of independent unit-change events may be limited, making it hard to detect small share changes.
As shown in TMP-009, same-shooter placebo and alternative play types can produce spurious signals; a design must include robust placebo tests.

prior_work.summary: Prior work indirectly addresses the question: a single defensive personnel change produces negligible shot mix shifts; shot mix can shift after timeouts; several attempts to isolate lineup/personnel effects on offense have failed due to talent confounds or measurement noise. The exact question of a full offensive five change has not been tested.

risks.text: Differences in player talent and stylistic roles between the old and new five will dominate any synergistic effect. Without a credible design to control for talent composition, the study risks attributing a mere composition shift to a general personnel effect.
The play-type classifier (especially the OTHER bucket) has known noise; systematic errors could create spurious shifts or hide real shifts.
Full five substitutions that occur in non-garbage time with the opposing defense unchanged may be uncommon, reducing the effective sample size and power to detect plausible effect sizes.

Previous artifacts (e.g., TMP-009) show that apparent play-type shifts can appear in placebo conditions. Without a built-in placebo (e.g., comparing the effect to timeout-only or to periods where the offense didn't change but the defense did), false positives are likely.
Multiple play types tested simultaneously increases type I error if not corrected.
Coaches may substitute after a run of bad possessions; the pre-change baseline may be an outlier, causing regression to the mean to masquerade as a personnel effect.

design.estimand: Average causal effect of a full offensive personnel change on the share of each major play type (DRIVE, SPOT_UP, PULL_UP, POST_UP, TRANSITION, CUT, OFF_SCREEN) over the next 5 possessions, compared to the 5 possessions immediately preceding the change under the same opponent defensive lineup and similar game state, controlling for talent composition.
design.unit: A full offensive substitution event: a dead-ball or live-ball sequence where the offensive team replaces all five players within 2 seconds of game clock, resulting in a new lineup that is disjoint from the previous lineup.
design.sample: All such events from NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 regular seasons and playoffs, excluding garbage time (score margin >25 in Q4), overtime, and events where the opponent also changes its defensive five simultaneously. Require at least 2 possessions in both pre and post windows.
design.power: Anticipate ~500-800 events; with 5 possessions each, minimal detectable difference of 1.5-2.0 percentage points per play type at β=0.2, α=0.05 (Bonferroni). Power will be stated after an audit of available events.
design.controls: Fixed effects for opponent defensive lineup (using a match ID), game quarter, score margin bin, and home/away. Additionally, include as a covariate the difference in the average per-100 possession shot frequencies of each play type for the players entering versus departing (taken from a separate season sample to avoid overfitting) to separate talent from synergy.
design.falsification: Two placebo tests: (1) Compare shot mix shifts after timeouts without a personnel change (using the same pre/post window design) — if the substitution effect is no larger, the study is inconclusive. (2) Randomly reassign event times to non-events and show no effect. Also, a within-event shuffle of play type labels should produce null results.
design.multiplicity: Principal analysis on a composite shot-mix measure (e.g., Euclidean distance from team-season baseline) to reduce multiplicity; secondary analysis on individual play types with Holm-Bonferroni correction.
design.decision_rule: Declare a personnel effect if the composite shot-mix distance significantly exceeds both zero and the timeout-placebo effect with p<0.05, and if the talent-adjusted difference in individual play types survives multiplicity correction in the expected direction (more diverse shot mix?). A null result will be interpreted as adequately powered non-support if the minimal detectable effect is below 1.5pp.
design.data_version: NBA stats API play-by-play and derived play-type records frozen as of 2025-11-02.

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-11-02, in the area of lineup and matchup effects):
Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["offensive lineup changes", "shot mix", "personnel effects", "lineup effects"], "methodological_questions": ["how to measure shot mix", "how to isolate personnel effects from confounding", "natural experiment design for lineup changes", "statistical power for shot mix shifts", "reliability of shot mix classification"], "query": "lineup changes shot mix personnel effects detection design"}}

reasoning_details.text:
We need to perform Stage 1: retrieval. Identify research concepts and methodological questions from the task statement.

Research question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects."

Interpretation: This is about lineup effects on shot mix. The hypothesis: altering the offensive unit (the five players on the floor) leads to changes in the distribution of shot types (shot mix). The underlying goal is to demonstrate that a research design (likely some quasi-experimental or observational method) can detect personnel effects using shot mix variation when lineups change. This is a feasibility/methodological check: can we detect personnel effects by seeing changes in shot mix when offensive fives change? So concepts: offensive lineup changes, shot mix (distribution of shot types/distance, or play types), personnel effects. Methodological questions: How to measure shot mix? How to isolate personnel effects from confounding (like opponent defense, game context, score, fatigue, coaching)? What design? Might involve comparing moments when a lineup changes vs. stable lineups, perhaps using substitution intervals. Key methodological concerns: MEASURE_RELIABILITY (shot mix classification), CONFOUNDING (defense, opponent, game state), SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (number of lineup changes). Also potential LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD if looking at future outcomes. RTM_SELECTION due to lineup changes often triggered by performance. EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: some lineups rarely used. So I'll list research concepts: "offensive lineup changes", "shot mix", "personnel effects", "lineup effects". Methodological questions: "how to measure shot mix", "how to isolate personnel effects from confounding", "how to define a lineup change", "natural experiment design for lineup effects", "statistical power for detecting shot mix shifts", "reliability of shot mix classification". The query should be concise: "lineup changes shot mix personnel effects detection".

Now call retrieve_history with those.

We need to produce a stage-2 assessment. Let's parse the retrieval results, integrate information, and then produce the final JSON output following the schema.

First, let's understand the research question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects."

So the hypothesis: Changing the offensive lineup (the five players on offense) changes the shot mix (i.e., distribution of shot types like pull-up, drive, spot-up, etc.), and this effect is detectable with the data we have. The goal is to decide whether this is testable with the available data (NBA 2022-25 seasons, per-game play-by-play, shot mix derived, etc.) and what has been established historically, risks, and design.

We have retrieval results. Let's examine them one by one:

1. FAM:SF-TMP-009: "PULL_UP exposure-effect diagnostics". It's about whether pull-up decline with exposure is defensive adaptation vs shooter selection/lineup artifact. Outcome: artifact. They found that with lineup FE, slope holding shot fixed was significant, but without lineup FE, effect shrinks to near zero, and placebo other play types also show effect, suggesting shooter-level confound, not lineup effect per se. It's relevant because it shows that when studying shot mix effects, lineup fixed effects can create artifacts or confounds. It's a risk of CONFOUNDING, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE.

2. FAM:SF-APPM-021: "Within-game tactical adaptation (halftime, crunch, post-run)". Descriptive. They looked at play-type mix shifts by halftime margin, crunch time, after runs. Found OTHER play type shifts big, but noted OTHER label is noisy (PT audit). Outcome: not a hypothesis test. Risks: LABEL_ERROR, MEASURE_RELIABILITY. Relevant to shot mix measurement reliability.

3. FAM:SF34: "Opponent lineup adaptation: shot mix when opposing rim big is off floor". Inconclusive. They tested: offenses attack rim more when opponent has no big. Result: DRIVE +0.82pp, POST_UP +0.43pp, 3PA -1.79pp, but rim <=4ft only +0.12pp (t=0.4), PPP +0.008 (t=1.1). Verdict: WEAK/SMALL. Sample: 1.07M possessions. Risk: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (though N is huge, the effect was small). This is about opponent lineup effect on shot mix, not offensive lineup change itself. But it is a design that looks at lineup change (opponent big off floor) and shot mix shift, so similar methodology. They found small effects, but significant in some play types. Inconclusive. So this suggests that detecting shot mix changes from a lineup change (even opponent) is possible but might be small.

4. FAM:SF-CHT-064: Defensive H2-adjustment reliability. Outcome: untestable. They found that defensive in-game adjustment trait (half-to-half change) has split-half r=-0.001, so not a reliable trait. This is about trait reliability of defensive adaptation, not directly about offensive lineup effects. But it underscores that team-level in-game changes might not be stable. Might be relevant to whether lineup change effects are consistent or just noise. Risk: MEASURE_RELIABILITY, MECHANICAL_FLOOR.

5. FAM:SF-TMP-005: Final checks: Design 5 placebo, defensive H2-adjustment trait reliability, etc. No result recorded, inconclusive. Some details about split-half reliability of H2-H1 change. Not very relevant.

6. FAM:SF-TMP-026: Defensive reorganizer 28-cell signature. Outcome: artifact. They found that a defender's effect on rewiring offense (DA_def) was actually below null, and size-adjusted split-half rho negative, suggesting artifact. This is about defensive lineup effect on offense shot mix? Actually "defender on the floor reliably rewires the opposing offense" - they found it's an artifact. So again, lineup effects (defensive) on opponent shot mix were not robust.

7. FAM:SF-TMP-023: After-timeout tactical play-type shift. Descriptive: after timeout, POST_UP +2.4pp, SPOT_UP +2.3pp, half-court PPP -0.0105. This is a different type of event (timeout) that changes play type. It suggests that play type mix does shift in certain situations, and the design can detect it (t-values high). But it's not about changing players, it's about a strategic decision. It's relevant because it shows that the methodology can detect a shot mix change from a discrete event (timeout). The question is whether changing the offensive five is a large enough event.

8. FAM:SF-APPS-087: Connector tangible impact. Outcome: rejected (null). They found no shielding effect, and lineup ORtg lift was a talent confound. Relevant because they tried to measure lineup-specific effect on efficiency (shot quality?), and found null. This might indicate that lineup effects on offensive performance are hard to detect over talent.

9. FAM:SF-APPA-066: TOV_FORCE matchup decomposition on four playoff games. Outcome: not a hypothesis test, untestable due to small sample. This is about player-level matchup effects, not lineup-level. But it illustrates issue of sparse exposure.

10. FAM:SF38: Defensive in-game adaptation to repeated play type (exposure slope). Inconclusive. They found only pull-up had within-game decline, while other play types had no effect. This is about adaptation to repeated exposure, not lineup changes. But it again shows that shot mix changes might be small except for pull-up, and that reliability is low (team trait split-half r +0.008). So any attempt to detect shot mix changes from lineup changes could face low signal.

Now we need to fill the schema. Let's start with research_concepts and methodological_questions. We'll list them based on the original question and retrieval.

Concepts: offensive lineup changes, shot mix distributions, personnel effects, lineup effect detection.

Methodological questions: how to measure shot mix (play type classification reliability), how to isolate personnel effects from confounding (talent, opponent), natural experiment design for lineup changes (e.g., substitution intervals, staggered rotations), statistical power for detecting small shifts in play type proportions, reliability of play type labels.

Now historical_evidence: list each retrieved record with its status as recorded. We'll pick the ones that are most directly relevant. Not all 10 need to be in historical_evidence? The instruction says "historical_evidence: only records returned by a tool, with the status as recorded; empty lists if nothing relevant was returned." But we should include those that are relevant to the question. The retrieval returned 10. We should include them but maybe we can focus on those that illuminate the question. The field expects an array of objects with id, status_as_recorded, finding. We can include several that have direct bearing on lineup effects on shot mix and design detection. I'll include:

- SF34: inconclusive, about opponent lineup adaptation, shot mix shift.
- SF-TMP-009: artifact, about pull-up effect being confound, no lineup effect.
- SF-APPM-021: not a hypothesis test, but mentions OTHER label noise.
- SF-TMP-023: not a hypothesis test, shows timeout causes play-type shift, so design can detect.
- SF38: inconclusive, exposure slope, only pull-up shows, small effects.
- SF-CHT-064: untestable, reliability of defensive adjustments, maybe not direct but caution.
- SF-APPS-087: rejected, connector impact null, lineup ORtg lift confounded by talent.
- SF-APPA-066: not a hypothesis test, small sample for player-level.

We need to ensure status_as_recorded exactly matches the record: "inconclusive", "artifact", "not a hypothesis test", "untestable", "rejected", "no result recorded". Use the exact string from record attributes: auto_outcome_status. For SF34: "inconclusive". SF-TMP-009: "artifact". SF-APPM-021: "not a hypothesis test". SF-CHT-064: "untestable". SF-TMP-005: "no result recorded". SF-TMP-026: "artifact". SF-TMP-023: "not a hypothesis test". SF-APPS-087: "rejected". SF-APPA-066: "not a hypothesis test". SF38: "inconclusive". I'll include a subset.

I'll include all? The output schema doesn't require all, but it's safer to include all returned records as historical_evidence? The instruction says "keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded)". So I should include all 10 records as historical_evidence. I'll do that.

For failed_approaches, I need to list records where the approach failed, and what failed. I can use records that have failure mechanisms like artifact, untestable, rejected, etc. I'll include: SF-TMP-009 (artifact due to confound), SF-CHT-064 (untestable due to low reliability), SF-TMP-026 (artifact), SF-APPS-087 (null due to confound), SF38 (inconclusive but might have issues). However, the field is "failed_approaches" with what_failed and why. I'll select those that represent methodological failures relevant to this question: SF-TMP-009: "using lineup FE to isolate shooter effect introduced confound", SF-CHT-064: "tried to measure defensive half-to-half adjustment as a trait but reliability ~0", SF-TMP-026: "defensive reorganizer signature turned out to be an artifact", SF-APPS-087: "lineup-level connector effect confounded by talent". Also SF-APPA-066: small sample, but that's a limitation. I'll include.

Now evidence_establishes: based on the retrieval, what does it establish? For example, that shot mix shifts from lineup changes (offensive or defensive) are generally small (SF34: rim share +0.12 with SE 0.295, PPP +0.008), that pull-up-specific effects can be confounded by shooter-level factors (SF-TMP-009), that play-type classifications (OTHER) are noisy (SF-APPM-021), that detecting lineup effects on shot mix is challenging and often returns small or null results unless confounded. It also establishes that some designs (timeout, opponent big off) can detect shifts but with modest magnitude. Also, the reliability of in-game adjustments is low. So the evidence establishes that the overall shot mix shift from lineup changes is likely tiny and may be hard to detect, and that confounding (talent, shooter identity) is a major issue.

Evidence_does_not_establish: it doesn't establish that offensive lineup changes never affect shot mix; few studies directly tested a full offensive substitution (all five players) on shot mix. The closest is SF34 (opponent big off) which is only one player change. And SF-TMP-023 (timeout) is a different event. So the question as posed—changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix—has not been directly addressed; we don't know whether a complete overhaul of the unit yields a detectable signal. Also, the data might be adequate but the specifics of sample size for many lineup changes? Not established.

Own_inferences: I need to add my inference. For example, that the question is highly vulnerable to confounding because when the offensive five changes, it's usually due to substitutions that bring in different talent levels, altering shot mix not because of synergy but because of individual player skills. To separate personnel effects from mere talent composition, one would need a design that compares lineups with similar talent but different "fit" or uses a natural experiment like staggered substitutions. The data likely have enough possessions to detect moderate shifts (~0.5-1 percentage point in a specific shot type) if the effect exists, but the risk of false positive from confound is high. Also, the play-type classification reliability might be a problem, especially for OTHER. So I'd suggest that while testable in principle, it's high risk and likely to produce either null or artifact.

Uncertainties: the amount of usable "offensive five change" events; we need to define what constitutes a change (full substitution vs gradual). How to define shot mix (share of each play type or a composite metric). The reliability of play type labels across seasons and teams. The appropriate control for opponent defense and game context.

Historical_effect: The historical evidence changed the decision? I think it did, because it shows past attempts to measure lineup-related shot mix effects have produced small, inconclusive, or artifactual results, and that measurement and confounding are major issues. So I'll say "yes", and explain.

Testability: I need to assign p_testable probability that question can be answered with stated data at useful power. I'd say it's moderately low, maybe 0.4, because the data are extensive, but from past evidence effects are small and confounding is hard to overcome. So p_testable = 0.4. Blocking constraints: list risk codes as objects with code and text. I'll include CONFOUNDING, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY (if we need many lineup combinations), LABEL_ERROR. I'll pick the most critical.

Prior_work: already_answered? Not directly. The retrieved work did not answer the exact question, but provides relevant insights. So I'll say "partly" or "no". "no"? Actually SF34 partly addresses but for opponent lineup. So "partly". cited: identifiers I'll list SF34, SF-TMP-009, SF-APPM-021, SF-TMP-023, SF38, etc.

Risks: similar to blocking constraints, but with more text.

Predicted_outcome: probabilities: supported (significant detectable effect) maybe 0.15, rejected (null with good power) 0.25, untestable (cannot be tested due to confounding) 0.30, artifact (spurious effect due to confounds) 0.20, uncertain (inconclusive) 0.10. Sum to 1.
